newsitem.title: UK: German Esso stations consider filing EC complaint.
newsitem.headline: German Esso stations consider filing EC complaint.

text.p: Contract disagreements may prompt some German petrol stations selling the Esso brand to file a complaint with the European Commission against the U.S.-based oil company, a group representing about one-third of the country's total stations said.

The Central Association of Petrol and Service Stations, which has a board meeting May 15, may eventually widen its complaint to include Royal Dutch/Shell Group, said Jurgen Ziegner, general secretary.
"The two companies we think are violating European regulations of vertical restraint are Esso and Shell and first we are considering filing a complaint against Esso," he said.
The move would mirror the decision by some Esso licensees in Great Britain to file a complaint with the EC earlier this year on the heels of last year's Pricewatch campaign in the U.K.
Esso, a unit of oil giant Exxon Corp, said on Monday that the EC had requested information from it in response to the complaint.
Pricewatch promises to match its lowest-priced competitors, which has left U.K. pump prices amongst the lowest in Europe but also squeezed downstream margins.

In Germany, the agreement between the oil companies and the petrol stations, called agency contracts, has given too much power to the oil companies in terminating their relationship at short notice, Ziegner told Reuters.

He also alleged that margins have been cut and rental costs raised in order to compensate for earnings in other Esso markets. German petrol stations are not protected from this under current European regulation, he said.

"What we don't have in Germany is a legal security for rented objects in the commercial sector so the contract can be terminated by both sides within three months to one year and that is the main problem we have," he said.
"What we think is that by such means the oil company has built up a power position which is not guaranteed by European regulations," he said.
The group also believes that a businessperson running a petrol station is not a "real agent" as understood in their agreements, since only a third of their gross margins come from fuel, Ziegner said.
"The problem we have with European regulation is that the mainstream opinion about article 85 of the Treaty of Rome is that it doesn't cover agency contracts," he said.
Ziegner said the group speaks for about 5,000-6,000 of Germany's 17,500 filling stations, and about 800 of an estimated 1,400 forecourts selling the Esso brand.
Germany's monopoly authority has already been contacted regarding the dispute, he said.
